heading: Remedies
memo_rationale: The existing limits are useful, but references to deleted §6.2.1 and potentially broader “obligations then owing” need to be reconciled with the new remedial structure.
memo_replacement: Buyer may enforce only the rights and remedies expressly permitted by Section 6, subject to Section 9 for any claim against a Guarantor and to applicable law. No provision in this Section expands the Purchased Receipts, accelerates ungenerated Receipts, or permits collection of Merchant’s retained share.
current_body: Upon any Event of Default, Buyer may pursue any remedy available at law (including those available under the UCC) or in equity to collect, enforce, or satisfy any obligations then owing, subject in every case to the limits in Section 6 — including the restriction in Section 6.2 on the availability of the remedy in Section 6.2.1, the notice and cure requirement in Section 6.1, and the aggregate limit in Section 6.3.
my_note: Housekeeping, but it must be done in the same pass as 053/054 or it dangles a reference to a deleted subsection.

heading: Events of Default
memo_rationale: The broad covenant, account, collateral-value, unrelated-contract, financing, and business-interruption defaults can undermine nonrecourse language. The existing overriding bankruptcy/business-failure exclusion is meaningful and should be preserved. A guarantor-termination notice is a default under §6.1.3, but it is not one of §6.2.1’s enumerated acceleration triggers; the prior finding overstates that direct link. The replacement deliberately narrows remedies beyond the minimum established in favorable NY cases. [A1–A4]
memo_replacement:
An Event of Default occurs only if Merchant (a) commits fraud in procuring or performing this Agreement; (b) intentionally diverts, conceals, or transfers Purchased Receipts that have actually arisen for the purpose of preventing their delivery to Buyer; or (c) knowingly sells or grants another person a conflicting interest in the same Purchased Receipts for the purpose of defeating Buyer’s ownership. Buyer shall give written notice identifying the conduct and supporting facts. For conduct capable of cure, no Event of Default occurs unless it remains uncured ten Workdays after receipt of notice. Buyer may apply to a court for temporary relief in accordance with applicable law.
Neither a decline or absence of revenue, delay in customer payment, ordinary business loss, good-faith closure, insolvency, bankruptcy filing by or against Merchant, bank or processor failure, nor loss of information access is itself an Event of Default. A missed estimate, reconciliation request, good-faith dispute, guaranty termination or nonrenewal notice, or default under another agreement is not itself an Event of Default. A breach of an administrative covenant may support proportionate lawful relief for proven direct loss, but does not make the uncollected Purchased Amount absolutely payable. Buyer bears the risk that Purchased Receipts may never arise. This Section controls inconsistent terms in this Agreement and incorporated documents, subject to mandatory law.
my_note: Adopt the narrowing. Fifth REFUTATION and it matters: guarantor termination under §6.1.3 is a default but is NOT one of §6.2.1's enumerated acceleration triggers — our register overstates a direct link that is not there. Correct it. Keep the existing overriding bankruptcy and business-failure exclusion, which is the best sentence in this contract.

heading: Remedies
memo_rationale: §6.2.1 accelerates and takes 100% for specified triggers, while §6.2.5 separately allows all-or-any processor collections without notice. Both require revision; editing only the explicit acceleration clause leaves a parallel sweep. NY decisions do not categorically prohibit acceleration, but the combined provisions create serious risk here. Limit recovery to proved loss and generated purchased assets; no confession, unlawful redirection, or self-help. [A1–A4, A7, A12]
memo_replacement:
After an Event of Default and any applicable cure period, Buyer may seek lawful judicial relief to recover Purchased Receipts actually generated and wrongfully withheld and proven direct damages caused by the specified conduct. Buyer must establish the conduct, causation, and amount of loss. The uncollected Purchased Amount is not automatically due and is not agreed liquidated damages. No remedy compensates Buyer for ordinary non-generation of future receipts or permits double recovery. Recovery attributable to the purchased pool reduces the Remaining Balance dollar for dollar.
The Specified Percentage does not increase on default. Buyer may give an Approved Processor accurate instructions to continue only the agreed purchased-share remittance, contemporaneously copied to Merchant, subject to the processor’s signed agreement and valid prior rights. Buyer may not redirect funds committed to another creditor or factor without legally sufficient consent or assignment. This Agreement authorizes no deposit-account debit, collection of all settlements, confession of judgment, or signing of process in Merchant’s name. Collateral enforcement is confined to Section 4.10 and applicable Article 9, judicial-process, and bankruptcy requirements. The Guaranty is enforceable only under Section 9.2. Reconciliation, refunds, accounting, the purchase cap, and all statutory defenses remain effective during enforcement. For a breach of an administrative covenant that is not an Event of Default, Buyer may seek only proportionate judicial relief for proven direct loss after written notice and at least ten Workdays to cure; that claim does not accelerate future receipts or expand the Guaranty. Costs are governed solely by Section 6.3.
my_note: §6.2.1 accelerates to 100%; §6.2.5 separately allows all-or-any processor collection without notice. Editing only the visible acceleration clause leaves a parallel sweep — the memo is right that these must move together. Limit recovery to proved loss and generated purchased assets.

heading: Costs of Collection
memo_rationale: Actual/reasonable costs, the 25% aggregate ceiling, no duplication, and no contractual interest are useful protections. However, payment on demand, internal administrative costs, all related agreements, and every guarantor broaden recourse. Statutory prejudgment interest does not necessarily use forum law or begin on demand. Require adjudication or settlement and preserve any mandatory reciprocal-fee rules.
memo_replacement:
To the extent permitted by law, Merchant shall reimburse reasonable, necessary, documented external attorneys’ fees, court costs, and collection expenses actually incurred to establish and enforce a valid claim under Section 6.2 or to defend a covered third-party claim under Section 7.9, only in the amount awarded by a court or expressly agreed in a written settlement. No internal overhead, unearned commission, percentage surcharge, cost allocated to an unsuccessful claim, or duplicate charge is recoverable. Buyer shall supply an itemized statement and supporting invoices. Guarantor liability is limited to costs attributable to a valid claim against that Guarantor under Section 9.2. Any mandatory reciprocal right to fees is preserved.
All enforcement costs under this Agreement and its incorporated documents together shall not exceed 25% of the Remaining Balance immediately before the conduct giving rise to the valid claim. This ceiling is not an agreed fee or evidence that a charge is reasonable. Costs do not increase the Purchased Amount or Remaining Balance and may not be collected through the processor split.
6.3.1 Statutory Interest. Prejudgment and postjudgment interest is recoverable only if, from the date and at the rate, authorized by applicable law or ordered by the court. No contractual default interest accrues, and an invoice or demand alone creates no right to statutory interest.
current_body:
Each Merchant and Guarantor shall pay to Buyer, on demand, all costs and expenses incurred by Buyer in connection with any Event of Default or the enforcement of Buyer's rights under this Agreement, the Guaranty, or any related agreement. Such costs and expenses are limited to amounts actually incurred and reasonable in amount, and include: (i) attorneys' fees; (ii) administrative or filing fees, expert witness fees, and costs of suit; and (iii) collection-agency commissions. Buyer shall on request furnish Merchant a reasonably detailed statement of the amounts claimed under this Section. Notwithstanding any other provision of this Agreement, the aggregate of all amounts recoverable from Merchant and Guarantor(s) on account of enforcement costs and expenses — under this Section, Section 4.10, Section 6.2.3, Section 7.9, and Appendix A combined — shall not exceed twenty-five percent (25%) of the undelivered Purchased Amount, and in no event shall Buyer recover the same cost or expense more than once.
6.3.1 Prejudgment and Postjudgment Interest
If Buyer becomes entitled to the entry of a judgment against any Merchant or Guarantor, prejudgment and postjudgment interest shall accrue at the statutory rate provided by the law of the forum, and Buyer claims no contractual rate. This Agreement is not a loan and Buyer does not charge interest on it.
my_note: The actual-and-reasonable standard, the 25% aggregate ceiling and no contractual interest are genuinely good and should survive the redraft. Fix payment-on-demand, internal administrative costs, and the reach to every guarantor.

heading: Required Notifications
memo_rationale: Receipt by certified mail cannot reliably satisfy a 24-hour deadline. Bankruptcy information is useful for stay compliance, but delayed notice must not become indirect bankruptcy recourse. Use practical notice and the revised operational notice channel. [A19]
memo_replacement: Merchant shall notify Buyer under Section 7.3 promptly after learning of a bankruptcy filing affecting Merchant, ordinarily within three Workdays where practicable, so Buyer can comply with applicable law. Merchant shall give reasonable advance notice of a planned sale described in Section 5.18, ordinarily seven calendar days where practicable. Failure or delay in notice does not itself accelerate any amount or create guarantor liability. Buyer shall independently comply with any stay, court order, or other legal restriction of which it has notice.
current_body: Merchant is required to give Buyer written notice within twenty-four (24) hours of any filing under Title 11 of the United States Code. Merchant is required to give Buyer seven (7) days’ written notice prior to the closing of any sale of all or substantially all of Merchant’s assets or stock.
my_note: Certified mail cannot satisfy a 24-hour receipt deadline — the clause is unperformable as written. And late bankruptcy notice must not become indirect bankruptcy recourse.
